why_in_two_sentences: Healthline covers all four trauma responses competently and PsychCentral's dedicated fawn page is solid, but both stay inside the definition-signs-recovery template. Ours gets inside the half second before you agree, separates fawning from people-pleasing and from freezing, explains why just-set-a-boundary backfires, and why wins do not transfer to the mother or boss who trained the pattern.
what_we_do_that_they_dont: Describes the mechanism at the half-second level before the agreement comes out, not just the behavior afterward
Differentials competitors lack: fawning vs people-pleasing, fawning vs freezing, charm and peace-keeping lies as fawn moves
Explains why boundary advice made things worse for people in this pattern
Explains why wins with safe people do not transfer to the specific people who installed the response
34 verbatim FAQs on the edge cases

above_the_fold.ours: H1 is the query, the short answer places fawning alongside fight/flight/freeze as moving toward the threat, then recognition sentences; direct and specific.
above_the_fold.theirs: PsychCentral opens with difficulty saying no and denying your own needs as the hook, names Pete Walker and his book in the first paragraphs; provenance arrives immediately.

questions_they_answer_that_we_dont: What types of trauma cause the fawn response?
trust_signals: Both competitors credit Pete Walker as the term's originator (with the book title) and show named medical reviewers; ours explains the mechanism deeply but never says where the term comes from.
one_change_with_most_traffic_impact: Credit the term's origin (Pete Walker, Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving) in the definition section; on a definitional query, provenance of the term is the cheapest authority signal both competitors show and we omit.
